stories.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: The Amorite asked how many kor of dates the resident picked from a palm tree on the Jordan and mocked the answer of sixty.
stories.turn: The resident revealed he was speaking only of one side of the tree.
stories.outcome: The Amorite's charge that the Israelites had ruined the land was answered.
stories.summary: An Amorite asked an Israelite how many kor they took from the palm tree by the Jordan. Told sixty, he scoffed that they had already ruined the land, since his people took 120. The Israelite replied that he had been counting only one side of the tree.

stories.event: On going up to Eretz Yisrael, then being ordained, then being seated on the intercalation council, he declared each time that he had been spared another curse.
stories.turn: Each step of his rise in the land freed him from one more curse.
stories.outcome: By the third appointment he said he had been spared three curses (the window ends there).
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had escaped one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was seated on the council that intercalates the calendar he said three.

stories.event: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry.
stories.turn: The man revealed he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
stories.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging him.
stories.summary: As Shmuel was crossing on a ferry, a man gave him a hand. Shmuel asked his business, and the man said he had a case. Shmuel told him he was now disqualified from judging it.

stories.event: While Ameimar sat judging, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he was judging, and a man brushed it off. Learning the man had a case, Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging it.

stories.event: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva. When he said he had a case, Mar Ukva declared himself disqualified from hearing it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket on Thursday instead of Friday.
stories.turn: The sharecropper admitted he had a case and brought it on the way; the rabbi refused it and recused himself, yet found himself mentally arguing the man's side.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed against bribe-takers, since he was biased even without taking anything.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper usually brought fruit on Friday but came Thursday, explaining he had a case. The rabbi refused the fruit, disqualified himself and appointed two scholars to judge. Pacing about, he kept thinking of arguments for the sharecropper, and cursed those who take bribes, since even he, who took nothing, was swayed.

stories.event: A man from far away brought him the first shearing.
stories.turn: The man admitted he had a case; the rabbi refused and recused himself but still caught himself favoring the man.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers, seeing how even an unaccepted gift biased him.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing from a distant town. Asked why he passed other priests, he said he had a case. The rabbi refused the gift, had two scholars judge, and found himself mentally pleading the man's case, and cursed those who accept bribes.

stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan refused the gift and disqualified himself (the window ends here).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish. When he said he had a case, Rav Anan refused the fish and declared himself disqualified from judging him.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The claimant gave a distinguishing mark and Rav Nahman knew Hasa was not wealthy.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded the goblet to the claimant.
stories.summary: A man had left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Before Rav Nahman, the man gave an identifying mark, and Rav Nahman, knowing Hasa was not rich, ruled the goblet was his.

stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The claimant gave a distinguishing mark and Rav Dimi was known not to be wealthy.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
stories.summary: A man had deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions. Rabbi Abba ruled for the claimant, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the man provided a distinguishing mark.

stories.actor: A dying man, Toviya and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to 'Toviya' and died.
stories.turn: A Toviya came to claim it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and takes the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After he died a man named Toviya came forward, and Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya receives it, without worrying about another Toviya.

stories.event: He came home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year was absorbed in study and did not come.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and came home each Yom Kippur eve. One year he stayed absorbed in study. His wife kept expecting him, and when he did not come a tear fell from her eye; at that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him, but one day stayed engrossed in study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The statement acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, came home each Shabbat eve, a pillar of fire preceding him. One week he stayed in the study hall; Rabbi Yannai saw no sign and said to overturn his bed, for if alive he would not miss his time. The words came true and Yehuda died.

stories.event: He arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the bride died when the contract was being written.
stories.turn: Suspecting a flaw, they investigated the lineages.
stories.outcome: They found Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from Shimi, David's brother (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's household, but the girl died as the marriage contract was being written. Rabbi asked if there was some disqualification, and the genealogies were examined: Rabbi came from David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's butler
stories.event: Seeing Mar Zutra blanch with craving, Rav Ashi put some of the king's food in his mouth.
stories.turn: Accused of spoiling the king's meal, Rav Ashi pointed to leprosy in the meat, which was found where he indicated.
stories.outcome: He explained to the Sages that he had seen a leprous spirit over the food.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as the butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra pale and fed him some with his finger. Charged with spoiling the meal, he claimed the meat was leprous; after a first search failed, he pointed to the spot and the defect was found. He told the Sages he had seen a leprous spirit over it.

stories.event: A Roman proposed and was refused, so he ate pomegranates before her without sharing until she fell ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He ate pomegranates again and told her to spit out the saliva; something like a green leaf came out and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He ate pomegranates in front of her until swallowing her craving made her ill. Then he offered to cure her if she married him; she agreed, he had her spit while he ate, a green thing came out, and she recovered.

stories.event: Visiting Benei Berak, he saw goats under fig trees with honey and milk dripping and mixing.
stories.turn: He realized this was the literal meaning of 'flowing with milk and honey'.
stories.outcome: He declared it so.
stories.summary: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees, honey oozing from the figs and milk dripping from the goats, mingling together. He said this is what 'a land flowing with milk and honey' means.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and later Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: The three sages were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot and divided it in thirds.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came and was served a peach he could hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: He cited the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste because of its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three sages visited a place and were brought a huge peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar came and the peach fit in his hand. He quoted the verse about a fruitful land turning to salt for its people's sins.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and later Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: In Gavla Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters as big as calves and told the land to withhold its fruit from the gentiles.
stories.turn: The next year the clusters had shrunk to the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya remarked on them, the locals told him to leave and not do what his colleague did.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw clusters like calves in Gavla and cried to the land to gather in its fruit rather than give it to the gentiles. The next year Rabbi Hiyya came and saw clusters like goats. When he commented, the locals told him to go away and not do as his colleague had.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
stories.event: After a first match failed, Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son shortened the delay, then married first; he spent twelve years away and she became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi worried what people would say, the son prayed for her, and she was cured.
stories.summary: When the bride from Rabbi Hiyya's family died, a genealogical check explained it. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, agreeing on twelve years of study before marriage, but seeing her the son asked to marry first, and his father compared his haste to God's. After twelve years away she had become barren; neither divorce nor a second wife was acceptable, so he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: He left for twelve years of study without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai.
stories.turn: Returning, he could not find his home; he followed his daughter, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed and she was revived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left Rabbi Shimon's wedding feast to study and stayed twelve years. Back home the paths had changed; at the river he heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and followed her. His wife saw him and died from the shock; he protested to God and prayed, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years of study he went to the local study hall and sent word home rather than surprise his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him, unaware they were father and son.
stories.outcome: He was saddened, thinking he could have had such a son had he stayed (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returned after twelve years and, to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mishap, waited in the study hall and sent word home. His son Rabbi Oshaya, whom he did not recognize, came and asked him sharp questions. Rabbi Hama grieved that had he been home he would have had a son like this.

stories.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive priestly status because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Questioned, he showed that a Levite read after the man, so it was as a priest.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that another was presumed a priest since he read first in synagogue. Asked whether that was as priest or as a great man, he said a Levite read next. Rabbi Ami accepted him as a priest on that basis.

stories.actor: A witness and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: A man testified that someone was a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: He showed that a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated him to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that another was presumed a Levite, having read second. Asked whether it was for his greatness, he answered that a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi confirmed him as a Levite.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of teruma distribution to confirm a priest and Rabbi Elazar challenged him; later the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yohanan gave the very objection Rabbi Elazar had given.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for citing Rabbi Yohanan without attribution.
stories.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest since he read first; Reish Lakish asked whether he had received teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked if priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same exchange occurred with Rabbi Yohanan making Rabbi Elazar's point. Reish Lakish looked angrily at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from bar Nappaha and did not say it in his name?

stories.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
stories.event: They bought a maidservant for perutot but, lacking cash, left a piece of silver as collateral.
stories.turn: Her price rose and the sellers wanted to back out.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled no acquisition had occurred.
stories.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons bought a maidservant, giving silver as collateral since they lacked coins. When her value went up the sellers sought to retract, and Rabbi Ami ruled that neither money nor collateral had effected the sale.

stories.event: He came home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year was absorbed in study and did not come.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi, who studied with Rava, came home each Yom Kippur eve. One year he stayed absorbed in study; his wife waited, and when he did not arrive a tear fell from her eye. At that moment the roof beneath him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him, but one day stayed engrossed in study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The words acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, returned each Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire. One week he stayed studying; Rabbi Yannai, seeing no sign, told them to overturn his bed, assuming death. His words came true and Yehuda died.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
stories.event: Rabbi's son's match with Rabbi Hiyya's family ended when the bride died, so Rabbi matched him with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son cut the delay and decided to marry first, and was ashamed before his father.
stories.outcome: His father reassured him that he had acted with his Maker's perception (the window ends mid-story).
stories.summary: When the girl from Rabbi Hiyya's family died before the contract, the genealogy explained it. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study first; seeing her, the son asked first for six and then to marry at once. Ashamed before his father, he was told he acted like God, who brought forward the Sanctuary.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
stories.event: Reclining in an upper room in Lod, they were asked whether study or action is greater.
stories.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study.
stories.outcome: All concluded study is greater because it leads to action.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in the loft of Nit'za's house in Lod when the question came up whether study or deed is greater. Rabbi Tarfon said deed, Rabbi Akiva said study, and all agreed study is greater because it brings one to deeds.

stories.event: Holding an orphan's beer, he delayed selling it until the Festival.
stories.turn: He accepted the risk it might sour.
stories.outcome: He reasoned it would fetch ready cash at the Festival.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and waited until the Festival to sell it, explaining that even if it soured a little it would bring in ready money then.

stories.event: Holding his orphaned nephew's wine, he was taking his own wine to Sikhra and asked Rav Ashi whether to take the orphan's too.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi said the orphan's wine is no better than his own.
stories.outcome: Ravina was told to go and take it along.
stories.summary: Ravina managed wine for his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to sell in Sikhra. He asked Rav Ashi if he could bring the orphan's along, and Rav Ashi told him to go, since it was no better than his own.

stories.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
stories.event: Their mother deeded her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening; Rav Sheshet ruled for Rami and Rav Nahman for Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman rebutted Rav Sheshet's priority argument, since hours are not written outside Jerusalem, and cited judicial discretion.
stories.outcome: When Rav Sheshet claimed discretion too, Rav Nahman said he himself was an appointed judge and Sheshet had not reasoned that way at first.
stories.summary: Rami bar Hama's mother deeded her property to him in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening. Each brother won before a different judge. Rav Sheshet said Rami's deed came first; Rav Nahman replied that hours are not recorded and he ruled by judicial discretion. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman said he was the judge and Sheshet had not reasoned that way.

stories.event: Two deeds for one property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'.
stories.turn: The loser protested; Rav Yosef said his deed could be from the twenty-ninth.
stories.outcome: The man asked Rav Yosef to write him something (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rav Yosef awarded a property to the holder of the deed dated the fifth of Nisan over one dated simply Nisan. The other protested, and Rav Yosef said his deed might be from the end of the month. The man then began asking the rabbi to write him a document.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his mourners
stories.event: Rabbi instructed that he not be eulogized in small towns.
stories.turn: They first thought it was to spare trouble, but seeing everyone come to the city eulogies they realized it was for his honor.
stories.outcome: They understood his true reason.
stories.summary: In his last instructions Rabbi named Gamliel Nasi and Hanina bar Hama head, and said not to eulogize him in the towns. They assumed he wished to spare people trouble, but when they eulogized him in the cities and everyone came anyway, they concluded he had said it for his honor.

stories.event: A Divine Voice declared everyone at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but the launderer who visited him daily had missed it.
stories.turn: Hearing this, he threw himself from a roof and died.
stories.outcome: A Divine Voice declared he too was destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice said all present were destined for the World-to-Come. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day; when he heard, he went up to the roof, fell and died. A heavenly voice announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

stories.event: She immersed and came up with a bone found between her teeth.
stories.turn: The bone was an interposition.
stories.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
stories.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house immersed, and afterward a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi made her immerse a second time.

stories.event: Walking on the road behind a woman, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda cited Rav's own ruling permitting it for upright men.
stories.outcome: Rav said he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not themselves.
stories.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking with a woman ahead of them, and Rav told Rav Yehuda to speed up to escape Gehenna. Rav Yehuda reminded him he had allowed it for men of good character; Rav answered that he meant people like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not the two of them.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya Arikha and his widowed mother-in-law
stories.event: After supporting her for twenty-five years, he refused her further sustenance and her marriage-contract payment.
stories.turn: Rabba bar Sheila ruled for her and authorized seizure of his property, and Rava upheld it, but Rava found the authorization defective when she claimed the produce.
stories.outcome: Rava denied her the produce because the document was miswritten.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya Arikha supported his brother's widow for twenty-five years, then refused both sustenance and her marriage-contract payment. Rabba bar Sheila ruled she had kept silent out of embarrassment and must be paid, and when Rav Hiyya ignored him, authorized seizing his property; Rava said the ruling was good. But when she asked Rava for the produce since then, he found the authorization omitted which property was the deceased's, ruled it invalid, rejected her scribal-error argument, and denied her the produce.

stories.actor: A woman in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
stories.event: Obligated to take an oath, she agreed to swear in town if the court first wrote her a document of rights.
stories.turn: Rav Beivai ordered it written.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappi mocked the ruling as an 'unfortunate' statement from the house of Eli.
stories.summary: A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court; her opponent asked that she swear in town, hoping shame would make her admit. She asked that her document of rights be written in advance, and Rav Beivai agreed. Rav Pappi derided him for saying unfortunate things, being of the doomed house of Eli.

stories.event: While judging, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man removed a feather from Ameimar's head while he sat in judgment. Learning he had a case, Ameimar declared himself disqualified.

stories.event: A man covered spittle before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man had a case.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva; when he said he had a case, Mar Ukva said he could not judge it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the fruit basket a day early because he had a case.
stories.turn: Though he refused it and recused himself, he caught himself arguing the man's side.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought the Friday fruit on Thursday, explaining he had a case. The rabbi refused, appointed two scholars, and found himself thinking up the man's arguments; he cursed those who accept bribes.

stories.event: A man brought him the first shearing from afar because he had a case.
stories.turn: He refused it and recused himself but still found himself favoring the man.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man from a distant place brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing, admitting he had a case. The rabbi refused and had two scholars judge, but kept thinking of the man's claims, and cursed bribe-takers.

stories.event: A man with a case brought Rav Anan fish, which he refused.
stories.turn: The man said he wanted no judgment, only to give a gift like first fruits; Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman inferred the man was Rav Anan's relative (the window ends here).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan small fish and said he had a case; Rav Anan refused. The man said he would forgo the judgment but wished to give the gift, likening it to first fruits; Rav Anan then accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note saying he was disqualified. Rav Nahman concluded the man was Rav Anan's relative.

stories.event: He spent the night in a study hall where a demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent.
stories.turn: With each bow of his prayer a head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon died and he told the townspeople they had endangered him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha spent the night in the study hall, and a demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent. Each time he bowed in prayer a head fell off. The next day he told the townspeople that without a miracle they would have put him in danger.

stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna and Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head cloth and learned he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see it again until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him. When he came without a head covering, he explained he was unmarried. Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face until he married.
